title: Portuguese Gulf
subtitle: 1507–1650 · Albuquerque's Choke-Point, the Ottoman Challenge and the Ya'ruba War of Liberation

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: A Portuguese protectorate over Hormuz, an Ottoman province in al-Hasa, and Oman's Ibadi revival

entries.label: Albuquerque makes Hormuz a Portuguese protectorate
entries.hint: Returning in force in 1515, Afonso de Albuquerque took Hormuz for good, built the Fort of Our Lady of the Conception and left the Hormuzi king on his throne as a puppet — Portugal keeping the fort, a garrison and a growing share of the customs.
entries.note: 'Comentários de Afonso de Albuquerque'; the 1515 settlement and the fort. Standard account: Bailey Diffie & George Winius, 'Foundations of the Portuguese Empire' (1977).
keywords: Fort of Our Lady of the Conception

entries.label: The Captains of Hormuz
entries.hint: The captaincy of Hormuz was one of the richest and most corrupt posts in the Portuguese empire — a three-year tenure in which a nobleman was expected to make a fortune from the customs, the cartazes and outright extortion. Misgovernment steadily hollowed the protectorate out.
entries.note: Portuguese administrative records; the notoriety of the Hormuz captaincy (Steensgaard, 'The Asian Trade Revolution of the Seventeenth Century', 1974).

entries.label: Portuguese Bahrain
entries.hint: A Portuguese-Hormuzi expedition seized Bahrain in 1521, killing the Jabrid governor Muqrin ibn Zamil. For eighty years the island and its pearl banks were held for Portugal by a resident agent and a garrison in the rebuilt fort.
entries.note: Portuguese conquest of Bahrain, 1521; the death of Muqrin. Slot, 'The Arabs of the Gulf 1602–1784' (1993), opens where this ends.

entries.label: The Ottomans annex al-Hasa and Qatif
entries.hint: Pushing down from newly conquered Basra, the Ottomans made eastern Arabia the province (eyalet) of Lahsa, ending Jabrid rule of the oases. Ottoman governors held al-Hasa and Qatif — never securely — for over a century.
entries.note: Ottoman conquest of al-Hasa in the 1550s; the eyalet of Lahsa. Khoury, 'The Ottoman Province of al-Hasa'; Mandaville's studies of Ottoman eastern Arabia.

entries.label: Shah Abbas takes Hormuz; Bandar Abbas founded
entries.loc: Hormuz; Gombroon / Bandar Abbas on the Persian shore
entries.hint: With English East India Company ships and gunners, Shah Abbas I stormed Portuguese Hormuz in 1622. The trade and the customs moved across to a mainland port he renamed Bandar Abbas; the island city never recovered.
entries.note: The Anglo-Persian conquest of Hormuz, 1622; Steensgaard (1974). The Hormuzi royal family was deported to Goa.

entries.label: The Ya'ruba imamate re-unites Oman
entries.loc: Rustaq and Nizwa; then the whole Omani coast
entries.hint: The Ibadi scholars elected Nasir bin Murshid al-Ya'rubi imam in 1624, ending the Nabhani centuries and the civil wars. He and his successor Sultan bin Saif welded Oman into a single state and drove the Portuguese out fort by fort, taking Muscat in 1650.
entries.note: al-Salimi, 'Tuhfat al-Ayan'; Wilkinson, 'The Imamate Tradition of Oman' (1987). The election of Nasir bin Murshid, 1624.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The taking of Bahrain, the Ottoman fleets, the fall of Hormuz and Oman's liberation war

entries.label: The conquest of Bahrain and the death of Muqrin
entries.hint: A combined Portuguese and Hormuzi force landed on Bahrain, defeated the Jabrid governor Muqrin ibn Zamil in a pitched battle and killed him. The richest pearl island in the world passed to the Estado da Índia.
entries.note: Portuguese accounts of the 1521 Bahrain campaign; Barros, 'Décadas da Ásia'.

entries.label: Piri Reis sacks Muscat and besieges Hormuz
entries.hint: The Ottoman admiral and cartographer Piri Reis brought a fleet from Suez, stormed Muscat's Portuguese garrison and laid siege to Hormuz, but withdrew to Basra without taking the fort. He was executed in Cairo for abandoning the campaign.
entries.note: Ottoman and Portuguese accounts of the 1552 expedition; Özbaran, 'The Ottoman Response to European Expansion' (1994).

entries.label: Sidi Ali Reis and the battle off Muscat
entries.hint: The last Ottoman attempt to break Portuguese sea power in the Gulf ended in a running fight off Muscat and a storm that scattered the Ottoman fleet. Its commander, Sidi Ali Reis, abandoned his ships and made an epic three-year overland journey home through India and Central Asia.
entries.note: Sidi Ali Reis, 'Mir'at ül-Memalik' ('Mirror of Countries'), his own memoir of the disaster and the return.

entries.label: Persia takes Bahrain
entries.hint: A local revolt on Bahrain against the Portuguese agent gave Shah Abbas the opening to seize the island. Bahrain became a Safavid province governed from Persia — and, under Persian rule, one of the great centres of Twelver Shia learning.
entries.note: The 1602 Persian takeover of Bahrain; the beginning of Safavid rule (to 1717). Cole, IJMES 19 (1987).

entries.label: The Anglo-Persian conquest of Hormuz
entries.hint: English East India Company warships blockaded and bombarded Hormuz while a Persian army besieged the fort by land. After two months the garrison surrendered. A hundred and fifteen years of Portuguese Hormuz ended, and the Gulf's trade capital moved to the Persian shore.
entries.note: Steensgaard, 'The Asian Trade Revolution of the Seventeenth Century' (1974); the EIC's share of the plunder and the Gombroon customs.

entries.label: The Ya'ruba expel the Portuguese from Muscat
entries.loc: Muscat (Al Jalali and Al Mirani forts)
entries.hint: Imam Sultan bin Saif's forces took Muscat's two Portuguese castles by storm, ending Portuguese rule in Oman. The Ya'ruba then built a navy and carried the war to Portuguese possessions in India and East Africa.
entries.note: al-Salimi; Portuguese accounts of the loss of Muscat, 1650. Bridges to the Oman, Bani Utbah & the Gulf folio.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The cartaz, the split customs of Hormuz, Ottoman tax registers and Oman's restored imamate

entries.label: The cartaz — a licence for the sea
entries.hint: Portugal claimed the right to licence all shipping in the western Indian Ocean. A vessel without a Portuguese cartaz, naming its cargo and forbidding it from carrying war goods or trading at rival ports, could be seized or sunk. It was a protection system enforced by gunfire.
entries.note: The cartaz / cartazes system (Pearson, 'The Portuguese in India', 1987); its enforcement from Hormuz.

entries.label: The divided customs of Hormuz
entries.hint: By treaty the Hormuz customs revenue was split between the puppet king and the Portuguese crown, with Portugal's share steadily enlarged. The arrangement made Hormuz one of the Estado da Índia's chief sources of income — and its administration a byword for graft.
entries.note: Portuguese fazenda accounts; Steensgaard (1974) on the Hormuz customs and its decline.

entries.label: The Ottoman defters of Lahsa
entries.hint: Ottoman surveyors registered the villages, palm gardens, mills and pearl-boats of al-Hasa and Qatif in cadastral tax registers, folding eastern Arabia into the empire's standard fiscal machinery. The defters are the first systematic census the region ever had.
entries.note: Ottoman tapu-tahrir defters for the eyalet of Lahsa; Mandaville, 'The Ottoman Province of al-Hasā in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries', JAOS 90 (1970).

entries.label: The restored Ibadi imamate under the Ya'ruba
entries.hint: Nasir bin Murshid's election revived the full Ibadi constitutional apparatus — an imam chosen by the scholars for knowledge and justice, a treasury, courts, and the duty of jihad against the occupier. The Nabhani model of hereditary kingship was formally repudiated.
entries.note: The Ya'rubid imamate and its constitutional basis; Wilkinson (1987).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Augustinians on Hormuz, Safavid Shiism on Bahrain and the Ibadi jihad in Oman

entries.label: The Augustinian mission at Hormuz
entries.hint: Augustinian friars built a convent and church on Hormuz and served the small Catholic community of soldiers, settlers, converts and Armenian Christians. After 1622 the order moved its Gulf base to Persian Bandar Abbas and Isfahan.
entries.note: The Augustinian and Carmelite missions in the Gulf and Persia; 'A Chronicle of the Carmelites in Persia' (1939); Alonso, on the Augustinians of Hormuz.

entries.label: Bahrain becomes a Safavid centre of Shia learning
entries.hint: Under Persian rule Bahrain flowered as a seat of Twelver scholarship, its ulama teaching, writing and feeding jurists into Safavid Iran. The 'Bahrani school' of hadith-centred jurisprudence took shape in this period.
entries.note: The Bahrani scholarly tradition under the Safavids; Cole, IJMES 19 (1987); al-Bahrani, 'Lu'lu'at al-Bahrayn' (biographical dictionary).

entries.label: Ibadi revival as a war of liberation
entries.hint: The Ya'rubid imams framed the expulsion of the Portuguese as a religious obligation, and the scholars who elected them tied Omani independence to Ibadi doctrine. Faith and statehood were re-fused in a way that shaped Oman for the next two centuries.
entries.note: al-Salimi; Wilkinson (1987). The religious framing of the anti-Portuguese struggle.

entries.label: Forced baptism and the reach of the Goa Inquisition
entries.hint: Portuguese practice in the Gulf ports included baptising the orphaned children of non-Christians and referring cases to the Inquisition tribunal at Goa. Coercive conversion was part of how the Estado governed its subject populations.
entries.note: The Goa Inquisition's jurisdiction over Hormuz; the orfãos practice (Boxer, 'The Church Militant and Iberian Expansion', 1978).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The bastioned fort — Hormuz, Bahrain and the castles of Muscat

entries.label: The Fort of Our Lady of the Conception, Hormuz
entries.hint: Albuquerque's fort at Hormuz was among the earliest European artillery fortresses in Asia — angled bastions, gun platforms, a cistern-fed garrison. Its ruins still stand on the island, the first thing a ship rounding into the Gulf would have seen.
entries.note: The Hormuz fort (Forte de Nossa Senhora da Conceição); Portuguese military architecture in Asia (Bocarro's 'Livro das Plantas', 1635).
keywords: Fort of Our Lady of the Conception

entries.label: Al Jalali and Al Mirani — the castles of Muscat
entries.hint: The Portuguese built two forts on the rocks flanking Muscat's harbour after a Turkish raid. Captured by the Ya'ruba in 1650 and held by every subsequent ruler of Oman, they remain the symbol of the city.
entries.note: Al Jalali (Fort São João) and Al Mirani (Fort Capitão); Portuguese construction 1580s; Peterson, 'Historical Muscat' (2007).

entries.label: Bahrain Fort in its Portuguese phase
entries.hint: On the ruins of the Dilmun and Islamic capital, the Portuguese raised a squat gun-fort with corner bastions. The layered mound at Qal'at al-Bahrain — Dilmun tell, medieval town, Portuguese fort — is now a single World Heritage site.
entries.note: Qal'at al-Bahrain / 'Bahrain Fort'; the Portuguese-period bastions; UNESCO World Heritage (2005).

entries.label: Bandar Abbas — a planned Persian port
entries.hint: Shah Abbas developed the fishing village of Gombroon into a customs port to draw the Gulf trade to the mainland. After 1622 it took Hormuz's role wholesale, with English and Dutch factories on its waterfront.
entries.note: The development of Bandar Abbas / Gombroon as the Safavid Gulf port; Floor, 'The Persian Gulf: A Political and Economic History of Five Port Cities' (2006).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Portuguese Décadas, a rescued Hormuzi chronicle and an Ottoman admiral's memoir

entries.label: The Portuguese historians of the Gulf
entries.hint: João de Barros's 'Décadas da Ásia', Gaspar Correia's 'Lendas da Índia' and Albuquerque's 'Comentários' between them give a detailed, if triumphal, narrative of the Portuguese Gulf — a major written source for the whole region's 16th century.
entries.note: Barros, 'Décadas da Ásia' (1552–1615); Correia, 'Lendas da Índia'; 'Comentários de Afonso de Albuquerque'.
keywords: João de Barros Décadas da Ásia

entries.label: Pedro Teixeira rescues the chronicle of the kings of Hormuz
entries.loc: written up in Antwerp; researched at Hormuz
entries.hint: The Portuguese traveller Pedro Teixeira translated the lost Persian dynastic history of Hormuz into Spanish and published it with an account of his own overland journey from India to Italy. Without him, the internal history of the Hormuz kingdom would be almost blank.
entries.note: Pedro Teixeira, 'Relaciones del origen, descendencia y succesion de los reyes de Persia, y de Harmuz' (Antwerp, 1610); trans. Sinclair for the Hakluyt Society (1902).

entries.label: Piri Reis and the Ottoman charting of the Gulf
entries.hint: Piri Reis's 'Kitab-i Bahriye' ('Book of the Sea') includes detailed charts and sailing directions for the Persian Gulf — Ottoman naval intelligence gathered as the empire prepared to contest Portuguese control of it.
entries.note: Piri Reis, 'Kitab-i Bahriye'; Soucek, 'Piri Reis and Turkish Mapmaking after Columbus' (1996).
keywords: Piri Reis Kitab-i Bahriye Book of the Sea

entries.label: The missionary reports as a Gulf archive
entries.hint: Augustinian and Carmelite friars sent Rome and Lisbon a steady stream of letters describing Gulf politics, trade, populations and religion. Written to inform policy, they are among the richest observational sources for the early-modern Gulf.
entries.note: 'A Chronicle of the Carmelites in Persia and the Papal Mission of the XVIIth and XVIIIth Centuries' (1939); Augustinian correspondence (Alonso; Gulbenkian).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Persian silk rerouted, the pearl banks taxed by new masters, and the rise of Gombroon

entries.label: The battle over the Persian silk route
entries.loc: Persia → the Gulf vs. → Ottoman Aleppo
entries.hint: Shah Abbas tried to divert Persia's raw-silk exports away from Ottoman Aleppo and down the Gulf to English and Dutch buyers. The struggle over which way the silk flowed made the Gulf a front in the Safavid–Ottoman economic war.
entries.note: Steensgaard (1974); Matthee, 'The Politics of Trade in Safavid Iran: Silk for Silver' (1999).

entries.label: Hormuz declines, Bandar Abbas rises
entries.hint: After 1622 the customs, the merchants and the shipping crossed from the island to the mainland port. Gombroon, with its English and Dutch factories, became the Gulf's commercial capital; Hormuz shrank back to a fishing anchorage.
entries.note: Floor, 'The Persian Gulf' (2006); the post-1622 shift of Gulf trade to Bandar Abbas.

entries.label: The pearl fishery changes hands but not rhythm
entries.loc: Bahrain and the eastern Arabian banks
entries.hint: Portugal taxed the Bahrain pearl fleet, then Persia did, then the local shaykhs. The divers, captains and merchants carried on through every change of overlord — the fishery was the one Gulf institution no empire could relocate.
entries.note: Portuguese and then Safavid taxation of the Bahrain pearl fishery; the continuity of the industry (Carter, 'Sea of Pearls', 2012).

entries.label: The English and Dutch companies arrive
entries.hint: The English East India Company opened a factory at Gombroon in 1623 with its share of the Hormuz spoils; the Dutch VOC followed. Two new, heavily armed commercial powers now operated permanently in the Gulf.
entries.note: EIC and VOC factory records for Gombroon and Basra; Steensgaard (1974).

entries.label: Muscat becomes Oman's window on the world
entries.hint: As Hormuz fell, Portuguese Muscat became the chief victualling and trade port of the lower Gulf. When the Ya'ruba took it in 1650 they inherited a fortified harbour city already plugged into the Indian Ocean economy — the base for their maritime empire.
entries.note: Peterson, 'Historical Muscat' (2007); Muscat's rise in the last Portuguese decades.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The angled bastion, the broadside galleon and the birth of an Omani navy

entries.label: The artillery fortress comes to the Gulf
entries.hint: Portugal ringed the Gulf with low, thick-walled forts whose angled bastions gave crossfire along every face — the state-of-the-art European answer to cannon, transplanted to Arabia. Local rulers studied and later copied them.
entries.note: Portuguese bastioned fortification in the Indian Ocean (Bocarro, 1635); the influence on later Omani fort-building.

entries.label: Naval gunnery and command of the Gulf
entries.hint: The broadside-armed carrack and galleon let a handful of Portuguese ships dominate a sea full of unarmed or lightly armed local craft. It was the same technology — this time in English hands — that broke Portuguese Hormuz in 1622.
entries.note: Guilmartin, 'Gunpowder and Galleys' (1974); the role of shipboard artillery in Portuguese and then English Gulf dominance.

entries.label: The Ya'ruba build a blue-water navy
entries.hint: To fight the Portuguese at sea the Ya'ruba imams bought and captured European-rigged ships and built large vessels of their own at Sur. Within decades this fleet was raiding Portuguese Diu, Bombay and Mombasa — Arabia's first modern navy.
entries.note: The growth of the Ya'rubid fleet; its later Indian Ocean campaigns (Risso, 'Oman and Muscat', 1986).

entries.label: Portuguese hydrography of the Gulf
entries.hint: Portuguese pilots produced roteiros — running sailing directions with soundings, bearings and coastal profiles — for the whole Gulf, the first systematic European charting of its waters and a template later powers built on.
entries.note: Portuguese roteiros of the Gulf (D. João de Castro's tradition); the roteiro genre (Cortesão, 'Portugaliae Monumenta Cartographica').

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A Gulf caught in the first world conflict — and the Armenian silk merchants who worked it

entries.label: The Anglo-Persian alliance against Hormuz
entries.hint: Shah Abbas offered the English East India Company a share of the Hormuz customs and half the plunder in exchange for the ships and guns to take the island. It was a deliberate partnership between an Asian empire and a European company against a third power.
entries.note: Steensgaard (1974); the terms of the 1622 Anglo-Persian cooperation.

entries.label: European embassies through the Gulf
entries.hint: Adventurers like the Sherley brothers and formal Persian envoys crossed between Isfahan and the courts of Europe, much of the traffic passing through the Gulf ports. The Gulf was a corridor for the diplomacy of the anti-Ottoman coalition.
entries.note: The Sherley missions; Persian embassies to Europe (Matthee; Loureiro).

entries.label: The Armenians of New Julfa in the Gulf trade
entries.loc: New Julfa (Isfahan) → Bandar Abbas → India, Europe
entries.hint: Shah Abbas resettled Armenian merchants at New Julfa outside Isfahan and gave them the Persian silk export. Their network ran the silk down to Gombroon and out across the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean — a diaspora trade diaspora working the Gulf.
entries.note: Aslanian, 'From the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean: The Global Trade Networks of Armenian Merchants from New Julfa' (2011).

entries.label: The Hormuzi royal family in exile at Goa
entries.hint: After the fall of Hormuz the last king and his household were deported to Goa on a Portuguese pension. A dynasty that had ruled the strait for three centuries ended as exiles in someone else's colony.
entries.note: The deportation of the Hormuzi royal house to Goa (Portuguese records; Aubin).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The seaborne empires collide — Portugal, the Ottomans, Safavid Persia and the northern companies

entries.label: Albuquerque's strategy of choke-points
entries.loc: Goa, Hormuz, Malacca, the Indian Ocean
entries.hint: Albuquerque set out to control the Indian Ocean not by conquering land but by holding its narrow gates — Hormuz for the Gulf, Malacca for the Straits, Goa as the hub, and (he failed here) Aden for the Red Sea. The Gulf's fate for 150 years was decided by this doctrine.
entries.note: Subrahmanyam, 'The Portuguese Empire in Asia 1500–1700' (1993); Albuquerque's choke-point strategy.

entries.label: The Ottoman–Portuguese contest for the Indian Ocean
entries.hint: The Ottomans, masters of Egypt and Iraq, fought Portugal for the sea routes from the 1530s — at Diu, in the Red Sea, and repeatedly in the Gulf. Neither could dislodge the other; the two empires settled into a stalemate along the coasts of Arabia.
entries.note: Özbaran, 'The Ottoman Response to European Expansion' (1994); Casale, 'The Ottoman Age of Exploration' (2010).

entries.label: Shah Abbas rebuilds Persian power
entries.hint: Shah Abbas I reorganised the Safavid army, moved his capital to Isfahan and turned Persia into a power able to project force to its coasts. The recovery of Bahrain (1602) and Hormuz (1622) were expressions of that revived reach.
entries.note: Blow, 'Shah Abbas' (2009); Newman, 'Safavid Iran' (2006).

entries.label: The Dutch and English East India Companies
entries.hint: Chartered joint-stock companies with their own fleets and forts entered the Indian Ocean around 1600 and quickly outcompeted the cash-strapped, over-extended Estado da Índia. Their arrival in the Gulf sealed the Portuguese decline.
entries.note: Steensgaard (1974); the structural advantages of the chartered company over the Estado.

entries.label: The Iberian Union and its end
entries.hint: For sixty years the Portuguese crown was held by the kings of Spain, and Portugal's empire was drawn into Habsburg wars against the Dutch. By the time Portugal regained independence in 1640, its Gulf position was already gone.
entries.note: The Iberian Union (1580–1640) and its effect on the overstretched Estado da Índia (Subrahmanyam 1993).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Married settlers and mixed families, the subject population under the customs squeeze, and a dynasty in exile

entries.label: The casados and mestiços of Hormuz and Muscat
entries.hint: Portuguese soldiers who married locally — often Christian or converted women — formed settled 'casado' households, and their mixed-descent children became a permanent Luso-Asian community in the Gulf ports, neither fully Portuguese nor local.
entries.note: The casado communities of the Estado da Índia (Boxer, 'The Portuguese Seaborne Empire', 1969); the orfãs del-rei sent to marry settlers.

entries.label: Living under the cartaz and the customs house
entries.hint: For the Gulf's Muslim majority, Portuguese rule meant paying to sail, paying at the customs house, restrictions on building mosques, and the constant risk of a captain's extortion. The revolts of 1521, 1529 and 1602 measured the resentment.
entries.note: Local grievances under Portuguese rule recorded in the revolts and in Ottoman appeals for intervention (Özbaran 1994).

entries.label: The Portuguese slave trade in the Gulf
entries.hint: The Portuguese trafficked enslaved East Africans, Ethiopians and others through their Gulf ports for domestic service, the forts and the galleys, adding a new current to the region's long-running Indian Ocean slave trade.
entries.note: The Portuguese Indian Ocean slave trade (Alpers, 'The Indian Ocean in World History', 2014); slaves in the Gulf garrisons.

entries.label: Women in the mixed households of the ports
entries.hint: Local and Armenian Christian women married into the settler community, ran households that bridged languages and faiths, and passed property and connections to mixed-descent children. Their role held the Luso-Asian port society together, though the sources barely name them.
entries.note: Inferential from casado household studies (Boxer 1975, 'Mary and Misogyny'); the near-invisibility of these women in the record.
